title: What Is a Capsule Wardrobe? Meaning and How to Build One
h1: What is a capsule wardrobe, and how do you build one?
excerpt: What is a capsule wardrobe? A small set of clothes that all work together. Where the idea came from and how to build one in 7 steps, with the 90/90 rule.
tldr: A capsule wardrobe is a small set of clothes, often around 30 to 40 pieces a season, chosen so nearly everything goes together. To build one, watch what you actually wear, sort everything, clear the maybe pile with the 90/90 rule, pick a palette, wear only the capsule for two weeks and only then fill real gaps.
body:
A capsule wardrobe is a small set of clothes picked so that nearly everything goes with everything else. You keep a limited number of tops, bottoms, layers and shoes in colours that work together, and you actually wear all of them. Popular methods land at about 30 to 40 pieces a season (Project 333 uses 33), but there is no official number.

Below: what the term means, where it came from, and a seven-step way to build one from the clothes you already own, including how to clear out with the 90/90 rule.

What is a capsule wardrobe, exactly?

The word "capsule" is doing the work here: something compact and self-contained. In practice, a capsule wardrobe has four traits.

  • The pieces combine freely. Most tops work with most bottoms because the colours and the level of formality line up. Five tops and four bottoms that all pair give you 20 combinations before you add a layer.
  • It fits the life you have now. Someone in an office four days a week needs a different capsule from someone who works from home and walks a dog twice a day.
  • There's a stable core. Jeans, a good coat, plain knitwear and everyday shoes stay put. A handful of seasonal or fun pieces rotate in and out.
  • It's mostly built from what you own. The first version usually comes out of your current wardrobe, not a shopping list.

It isn't a uniform of grey basics, and it doesn't mean throwing out everything that doesn't fit the plan. Plenty of capsules are full of colour and print; the colours just agree with each other.

You'll also see brands launch a "capsule collection". That's a related idea: a small, self-contained line from a designer or retailer, and it has no set size either.

Where the idea came from

Susie Faux, who ran a boutique called Wardrobe in London's West End, is credited with popularising the term in the 1970s, although Wikipedia notes that it had already appeared in American publications in the 1940s. Her idea was a few essential pieces that wouldn't go out of fashion, such as trousers, a skirt and a good coat, topped up each season with a handful of newer things.

In 1985 the American designer Donna Karan launched Seven Easy Pieces: a bodysuit, a tailored jacket, a skirt, trousers, a cashmere jumper, a leather jacket and an evening look, meant to take a working woman from office to evening and weekday to weekend. Her brand still describes it as the original capsule collection.

The idea found a much bigger audience online. Courtney Carver's Project 333 challenged people to dress with 33 items for three months, and bloggers such as Caroline Rector of Un-fancy published their 37-piece seasonal capsules piece by piece. Most of the numbers you'll see quoted today come from those two.

Why people switch to a capsule wardrobe

Getting dressed gets quicker. With fewer pieces that all work together, there are fewer bad combinations to rule out at 7am.

You wear more of what you own. In a 2022 survey of more than 6,000 UK adults, the charity WRAP found that about a quarter of the clothes in the average wardrobe (26%, or 31 items) hadn't been worn for at least a year. A capsule puts those pieces in front of you, so they either get worn or move on.

Shopping changes too. Once you know your colours and what each new piece has to go with, it's easier to walk past something that would only work with one outfit.

There's an environmental case as well. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation says the equivalent of one truckload of clothing is landfilled or burned every second, and that clothing use, the number of times a garment is worn, has fallen by almost 40% in 15 years. Wearing things more often is one of the few fixes that costs nothing.

The downsides are real but manageable. The first edit takes an afternoon or two, a tight capsule can feel repetitive by the end of a season, and if clothes are your hobby, a strict count can take the fun out of it. Looser approaches such as the 70/30 split exist for exactly that reason; our comparison of capsule wardrobe rules covers them.

Capsule wardrobe vs minimalist wardrobe

The two overlap, but they aren't the same thing. Minimalism is a broad aim: own less. A capsule is a method: a defined set of pieces that combine, usually reviewed each season.

Capsule wardrobeMinimalist wardrobe
Main goalClothes that combine into many outfitsOwning less overall
SizeOften a target number per seasonAs few pieces as you're comfortable with
ColourAny palette, as long as it's coherentOften neutral, but not necessarily
SeasonsUsually a fixed core plus rotating seasonal piecesOften one year-round set

You can have a minimalist wardrobe that isn't a capsule (20 pieces that don't really go together) and a capsule that isn't especially minimal (a 50-piece year-round set for someone with a varied week). Our minimalist wardrobe guide goes further into the second approach.

How to build a capsule wardrobe, step by step

The order matters. Most capsules that fail start with shopping. This version starts with looking and only ends with buying, if at all. Expect the first edit to take an afternoon and the whole capsule to settle over a season.

1. Watch how you actually dress for two weeks

Before moving anything, note what you wear each day in a phone note or a notebook. Then look back at the last month of your calendar and count the kinds of days you had: office, remote work, school runs, gym, dinners, weddings. A typical split might be four office days, one day at home, and a weekend of errands with one evening out. Build the capsule around those proportions, not around the life you'd like to have.

2. Take everything out and sort it

Empty the wardrobe, the drawers and the chair in the corner. Put each piece in one of four piles:

  1. Keep: it fits now, you've worn it recently, and you feel good in it.
  2. Maybe: you like it but aren't sure it earns a place.
  3. Let go: it doesn't fit, doesn't suit your life, or you dread wearing it.
  4. Repair: a missing button, a dropped hem, worn-down heels. Book the repair this month or move it to "let go".

Keep out-of-season clothes in their own pile for now. A wool coat in July isn't clutter.

3. Clear the maybe pile with the 90/90 rule

The maybe pile is where most people stall. The 90/90 rule, from The Minimalists, gives you two questions for each piece:

  1. Have I worn this in the last 90 days?
  2. Will I wear it in the next 90 days?

If both answers are no, it goes. The Minimalists say the window can stretch to 120 days or six months if that suits you better, as long as you answer honestly. For clothes, a few adjustments help:

  • Judge seasonal pieces against their own season. Shorts you didn't wear all last summer fail. A heavy coat in spring doesn't.
  • "Someday" isn't a yes. "I might go somewhere smart" doesn't count. "My cousin's wedding is on 14 December" does.
  • Keep a small sentimental box. A few pieces kept for memory rather than wear are fine, as long as the box has a limit.
  • Use a holding box if you're torn. Seal it, write today's date on the lid and put it out of sight. If you haven't opened it in 90 days, donate it without looking inside.

For what leaves: sell anything in good condition, give to a charity or clothes swap that will actually use it, and send worn-out pieces to textile recycling rather than the bin.

4. Choose a colour palette from what survived

Look at the keep pile and notice which colours already dominate. Most capsules work with two or three neutrals and one or two accents. Navy, grey and white with olive is one example; black, cream and camel with burgundy is another. Patterns are fine if they share those colours, so a navy-and-white stripe sits happily in the first palette. Anything that clashes with everything else goes back to the maybe pile.

5. Set your core and pick a number

Choose the pieces that cover your usual week: everyday tops, one or two smarter tops, knitwear, two or three bottoms, a layer that smartens things up, a coat for your weather and three or four pairs of shoes. Our capsule wardrobe essentials checklist lists the usual candidates by category.

A number keeps you honest. If you're unsure, start with about 30 pieces for one season, not counting underwear, sleepwear and gym kit, and adjust from there. We break down how many pieces a capsule wardrobe needs by lifestyle separately.

6. Wear only the capsule for two weeks

Box up or move everything else out of sight and dress only from the capsule. Put together ten outfits on the first day, take a photo of each, and keep notes: the piece you reached for every day, the one you avoided, the moment you wished you had something else. A grey sweatshirt that works with all three bottoms is pulling its weight. A patterned shirt that only goes with one pair of trousers isn't.

If you'd rather keep that inventory on your phone: FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet. You photograph each piece, it tags the type, colour, pattern, season and formality, and it suggests complete outfits for an occasion using only clothes you own. You can join the early-access list to hear when it opens.

7. Fill real gaps slowly

After two weeks the gaps are specific: "a plain top that works under the blazer", not "more tops". Write each one down with the colour, the fit and what it has to go with. Buy one at a time, and only if the new piece works with at least three things you already own. From then on, one in, one out keeps the size steady.

Keeping it working each season

Every three months or so, swap out seasonal pieces, check the core for wear and tear, and run the 90/90 questions over anything you didn't touch. Where winters are cold, a common approach is a year-round core plus eight to twelve pieces that swap between seasons. Somewhere warm all year, one capsule may be enough.

If a capsule starts drifting back to a full wardrobe, it's usually one of a few predictable causes, from purging too much on day one to buying a whole new wardrobe at once. They're covered in capsule wardrobe mistakes to avoid.

faq.a: The term is usually credited to Susie Faux, who ran the London boutique Wardrobe in the 1970s and promoted a small core of timeless pieces topped up each season. The phrase had already appeared in American publications in the 1940s, though. Donna Karan's 1985 Seven Easy Pieces collection made the idea famous in the US, and blogs such as Project 333 later spread it online.

faq.q: What is the 90/90 rule for clothes?
faq.a: The 90/90 rule, from The Minimalists, asks two questions about each piece: have you worn it in the last 90 days, and will you wear it in the next 90? If both answers are no, let it go. Judge seasonal clothes against their own season, and only count specific plans, such as a wedding with a date, as a yes to the second question.

faq.q: How many pieces do you need for a capsule wardrobe?
faq.a: There's no fixed number. Popular methods use 30 to 40 pieces per season: Project 333 allows 33 items including shoes and accessories, and Un-fancy's well-known capsules had 37. Someone working from home in a mild climate may manage with 25, while a varied week in a four-season climate can need 40 or more. Underwear, sleepwear and gym clothes usually don't count.

faq.q: What is the difference between a capsule wardrobe and a minimalist wardrobe?
faq.a: Minimalism is a general aim to own less. A capsule wardrobe is a specific method: a defined set of pieces chosen to combine with each other, usually with a target size and a review each season. Most capsules are fairly minimal, but a minimalist wardrobe isn't automatically a capsule if its pieces don't work together.

faq.q: How long does it take to build a capsule wardrobe?
faq.a: The first sort takes an afternoon or a weekend. Getting to a capsule you're happy with usually takes a season, because you need a couple of weeks of wearing it to see which pieces earn their place and which gaps are real. Filling those gaps one item at a time spreads the cost and avoids panic buying.

faq.q: Do you have to get rid of clothes to start a capsule wardrobe?
faq.a: No. You can box up everything outside the capsule and store it for a season instead of donating it straight away, which is how Project 333 works. After three months you'll know which few pieces you actually missed. Those come back, and the rest can be sold or donated with far less second-guessing.
